fields.Front: How does ELT differ from ETL?
fields.Back: In ELT, raw data is loaded into the target system (e.g. a warehouse/lake) first, and transformed afterward using the target's own compute — instead of transforming before loading.

fields.Front: What happens in the "Extract" stage of ETL?
fields.Back: Raw data is pulled from one or more source systems (databases, APIs, files, etc.) into a staging area, generally with minimal transformation.

fields.Front: What happens in the "Transform" stage of ETL?
fields.Back: Extracted data is cleaned, validated, reshaped, joined, and enriched into the schema/format the destination requires.

fields.Front: What happens in the "Load" stage of ETL?
fields.Back: The transformed data is written into the target system (e.g. data warehouse or database) for downstream use.

fields.Front: What does it mean for an ETL pipeline step to be "idempotent"?
fields.Back: Running it multiple times with the same input produces the same end result as running it once — no duplicate or corrupted data from retries or re-runs.

fields.Front: Why is idempotency important for ETL pipelines?
fields.Back: Failures and retries are common in pipelines; idempotent steps can be safely re-run after a failure without creating duplicates or inconsistent state.

fields.Front: What's the difference between batch and streaming data processing?
fields.Back: Batch processes data in discrete, scheduled chunks (e.g. hourly/daily); streaming processes data continuously, record-by-record or in micro-batches, as it arrives.

fields.Front: What is an "incremental load" in ETL?
fields.Back: Loading only new or changed data since the last run (e.g. via a timestamp or change-tracking column), instead of reprocessing the full dataset every time.

fields.Front: Why prefer incremental loads over full reloads for large datasets?
fields.Back: They're much faster and cheaper — less data to extract, transform, and load, and lower load placed on source systems — than reprocessing everything on every run.

fields.Front: Name two common data quality checks run within an ETL pipeline.
fields.Back: e.g. null/missing-value checks, schema/type validation, duplicate detection, and range or referential-integrity checks.

fields.Front: What is Microsoft Fabric, at a high level?
fields.Back: A unified, end-to-end SaaS analytics platform (built on OneLake) combining data engineering, data integration/ETL pipelines, data warehousing, and Power BI reporting in one workspace.

fields.Front: In Microsoft Fabric, what is OneLake?
fields.Back: A single, unified, tenant-wide data lake (built on ADLS Gen2) underlying all Fabric workloads, so data doesn't need to be copied between engines.

fields.Front: What role does orchestration play in a data pipeline?
fields.Back: It schedules and sequences pipeline jobs, manages dependencies between them, and handles retries/failure recovery (e.g. via Airflow or Fabric/Data Factory pipelines).

fields.Front: In the COMPLIANCE360 project, what did the Python ETL pipeline on MS Fabric do?
fields.Back: Extracted and transformed compliance-related data, applied custom scoring algorithms to it, and loaded the results for a React front-end to display.

fields.Front: What is a "scoring algorithm", in the context of the COMPLIANCE360 ETL pipeline?
fields.Back: Custom logic run in the Transform stage that computes a numeric compliance/risk score for each record based on defined rules or weighted criteria.

fields.Front: How do you express an idempotent load step as an "upsert" (insert-or-update) instead of a plain insert?
fields.Back:
INSERT INTO target (id, val)
VALUES (1, 'x')
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET val = EXCLUDED.val;
Extract, Transform, Load — data is pulled from sources, transformed to the target format, and then loaded into the destination system.

fields.Text: A well-known reliability property for pipeline transactions is {{c1::ACID}}: {{c2::Atomicity}}, {{c3::Consistency}}, {{c4::Isolation}}, and {{c5::Durability}}.
fields.Extra: Many big-data/streaming pipelines instead trade strict ACID guarantees for eventual consistency at scale.
